foxglove.habit: Upright, clump-forming biennial or short-lived perennial. Reaches 1–1.5m in height.
foxglove.features: Tall spires of bell-shaped flowers; soft, hairy, mid-green basal rosettes in the first year.
foxglove.flowers: Tubular, nodding bells in shades of purple, pink, or white with spotted throats, May–July.
foxglove.conditions: Partial shade to full sun; prefers moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; hardy to -20°C.
foxglove.care: Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage a second flush or leave for self-seeding. Cut back to ground in autumn.
facts: Source of digitalin, used in heart medication, but the plant is highly toxic if ingested.
Folklore suggests foxes wore the flowers on their paws to silence their movements while hunting.

iris.habit: Herbaceous perennial with a creeping rhizomatous habit; sword-like fans of grey-green foliage.
iris.features: Architectural foliage provides vertical interest; striking 'bearded' flower structure.
iris.flowers: Exotic three-petaled blooms with 'falls' and 'standards' in almost every color; peaks May–June.
iris.conditions: Full sun (rhizomes need baking); neutral to lime-rich, well-drained soil; very hardy.
iris.care: Divide rhizomes every 3-4 years after flowering. Trim leaves to a fan shape in autumn to prevent wind rock.
facts: Named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow, Iris, who acted as a messenger between heaven and earth.
The 'Fleur-de-lis' symbol of French royalty is a stylized representation of the iris.

tulip.habit: Spring-flowering bulbous perennial; upright stems ranging from 10cm to 70cm.
tulip.features: Broad, glaucous green leaves; sleek, symmetrical goblet-shaped blooms.
tulip.flowers: Vast range of colors (except true blue) and forms (lily-flowered, parrot, fringed); April–May.
tulip.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; benefits from a sheltered spot to prevent wind damage.
tulip.care: Plant bulbs deep (3x height) in late autumn (November) to avoid 'Tulip Fire' fungus. Deadhead after flowering.
facts: In 17th-century Holland, 'Tulip Mania' caused bulb prices to exceed the cost of a house.
Tulip petals are edible and can be used in salads, though bulbs are toxic.

peony.habit: Bushy herbaceous perennial or woody shrub (Tree Peony); long-lived and substantial.
peony.features: Deeply divided dark green foliage; new shoots emerge as striking deep red 'noses' in spring.
peony.flowers: Large, often fragrant, bowl-shaped flowers in white, pink, or crimson; peaks May–June.
peony.conditions: Full sun to dappled shade; deep, fertile, moist but well-drained soil; hardy and reliable.
peony.care: Provide support for heavy flower heads in spring. Cut back herbaceous types to ground level in autumn.
facts: Peonies can live for over 100 years if left undisturbed in the right conditions.
In Chinese culture, it is known as the 'King of Flowers' and symbolizes honor and wealth.

camellia.habit: Evergreen shrub or small tree; dense, rounded habit with glossy, leathery dark green leaves.
camellia.features: Provides structural greenery year-round; blooms during the bleakest months of late winter.
camellia.flowers: Rose-like blooms in white, pink, or red; appear February–April. Avoid early morning sun which burns frosted buds.
camellia.conditions: Partial shade; acidic, moist, well-drained soil (ericaceous); sheltered, west or north-facing aspect.
camellia.care: Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Feed with ericaceous fertilizer in spring and early summer.
facts: The tea we drink (Camellia sinensis) is a close relative of the ornamental camellia.
In the 19th century, they were the ultimate luxury flower, often worn in buttonholes of formal attire.

magnolia.habit: Deciduous or evergreen tree/shrub; often spreading and architectural with smooth grey bark.
magnolia.features: Fuzzy, velvet-like flower buds in winter; large, dramatic leaves follow the spring bloom.
magnolia.flowers: Large star-shaped or tulip-shaped blooms in white, pink, or purple; March–May before leaves appear.
magnolia.conditions: Full sun or dappled shade; neutral to acidic soil; sheltered from cold winds to protect flowers.
magnolia.care: Minimal pruning required; remove crossing or dead branches in mid-summer. Mulch annually in spring.
facts: Magnolias are among the most ancient flowering plants, existing before bees (they are pollinated by beetles).
The flower represents dignity and perseverance due to its ability to survive for millennia.

wisteria.habit: Vigorous deciduous woody climber; requires strong support for its twining woody stems.
wisteria.features: Pinnate green leaves that turn yellow in autumn; impressive, gnarled trunks as the plant ages.
wisteria.flowers: Long, drooping racemes (up to 30cm) of fragrant, pea-like mauve or white flowers; May–June.
wisteria.conditions: Full sun for best flowering; fertile, moist, well-drained soil; south or west-facing walls.
wisteria.care: Prune twice yearly: in summer (July/August) cut long shoots to 5-6 buds; in winter (January) cut to 2-3 buds.
facts: Wisteria can take up to 20 years to flower if grown from seed; always buy grafted plants.
A single wisteria plant in Sierra Madre, California, is known as the 'largest blossoming plant in the world'.

sunflower.habit: Fast-growing annual herb; can reach 1m to 4m depending on variety.
sunflower.features: Tall, thick hairy stems with large, heart-shaped, rough leaves.
sunflower.flowers: Large composite heads with yellow ray florets and dark central discs; July–September.
sunflower.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, fertile soil; requires plenty of water during growth.
sunflower.care: Sow in April. Stake tall varieties. Leave heads in autumn for birds or harvest seeds.
facts: Sunflowers display heliotropism, turning their heads to follow the sun across the sky.
A single sunflower can contain up to 2,000 seeds.

hydrangea.habit: Deciduous shrub with a rounded, bushy habit; typically 1–2m tall.
hydrangea.features: Large, ovate, serrated leaves; attractive dried flower heads provide winter interest.
hydrangea.flowers: Large mopheads or lacecaps in blue, pink, or white; July–October.
hydrangea.conditions: Partial shade; moist, well-drained soil. Soil pH affects color (acid for blue, alkaline for pink).
hydrangea.care: Prune in spring, cutting back old flower heads to just above a pair of strong buds.
facts: The name comes from Greek 'hydor' (water) and 'angos' (vessel), referring to its water-loving nature.
In Japan, hydrangeas are associated with heartfelt emotion and apologies.

oleander.habit: Vigorous evergreen shrub or small tree; upright and mounding to 2–4m.
oleander.features: Narrow, leathery, willow-like dark green leaves; drought and salt tolerant.
oleander.flowers: Funnel-shaped blooms in clusters of white, pink, red, or apricot; June–September.
oleander.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; very heat tolerant; hardy to -5°C (needs winter protection in cold zones).
oleander.care: Prune in late winter to maintain shape. Wear gloves as all parts are highly toxic.
facts: One of the most poisonous commonly grown garden plants; even the smoke from burning it is toxic.
It is the official flower of the city of Hiroshima, as it was the first to bloom after the 1945 bombing.

snapdragon.habit: Short-lived perennial usually grown as an annual; upright spikes 15cm to 1m tall.
snapdragon.features: Lance-shaped leaves; unique 'hinged' flower structure that 'snaps' open when squeezed.
snapdragon.flowers: Multi-colored spikes in almost every shade except blue; June–October.
snapdragon.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, fertile soil; prefers cooler summer temperatures.
snapdragon.care: Pinch out young plants to encourage bushiness. Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering.
facts: The name 'Antirrhinum' means 'like a nose' in Greek.
Ancient people believed snapdragons could ward off witchcraft and aging.

nasturtium.habit: Vigorous annual; can be trailing, climbing (to 2m), or compact and mounding.
nasturtium.features: Distinctive circular (peltate) light green leaves; edible peppery flavor.
nasturtium.flowers: Trumpet-shaped blooms in brilliant orange, yellow, and red; June until first frost.
nasturtium.conditions: Full sun; poor soil actually encourages more flowers over foliage; well-drained.
nasturtium.care: Sow directly in May. Very easy care; do not over-fertilize. Watch for black bean aphids.
facts: Both the leaves and flowers are edible, tasting similar to watercress.
They are excellent companion plants, used as a 'trap crop' to lure pests away from vegetables.

pansy.habit: Low-growing, clump-forming short-lived perennial often grown as an annual.
pansy.features: Heart-shaped, scalloped leaves; iconic 'face' markings on the petals.
pansy.flowers: Large, flat-faced blooms in a vast array of colors and bicolors; peaks in spring and autumn.
pansy.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; moist, well-drained soil; very cold hardy.
pansy.care: Deadhead to keep flowers coming. Water regularly in dry spells. Plant in autumn for spring color.
facts: The name comes from the French 'pensée', meaning 'thought' or 'remembrance'.
Pansies were the first flower used in large-scale commercial hybridizing.

valerian.habit: Tall, upright herbaceous perennial; reaching 1m to 1.5m.
valerian.features: Pinnate, deeply toothed foliage; fern-like appearance at the base.
valerian.flowers: Small, scented pale pink or white flowers in dense terminal clusters; June–August.
valerian.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; prefers moist, heavy soils; very hardy.
valerian.care: Cut back after flowering to prevent self-seeding. Divide in spring or autumn.
facts: The root has been used since ancient times as a sedative and sleep aid.
Cats are often as attracted to valerian as they are to catnip.

thyme.habit: Low-growing, woody evergreen sub-shrub or carpeting groundcover.
thyme.features: Tiny, highly aromatic grey-green leaves; drought-tolerant and rugged.
thyme.flowers: Clusters of tiny tubular white to pale purple flowers; June–August.
thyme.conditions: Full sun; poor, gritty, very well-drained soil; hates winter wet.
thyme.care: Lightly trim after flowering to keep it compact. Replace plants every 3-5 years as they go woody.
facts: In ancient Greece, thyme was a symbol of courage; soldiers would bathe in thyme water before battle.
It is a primary source of thymol, a powerful natural antiseptic.

lavender.features: Silver-grey aromatic foliage year-round; provides structure in winter.
lavender.flowers: Violet-blue to pale lilac spikes, June–August; highly attractive to bees.
lavender.conditions: Full sun, excellent drainage, alkaline to neutral soil; extremely drought tolerant.
lavender.care: Cut back to new growth in April; avoid cutting into old wood. Trim spent flowers in late summer.
facts: Name from Latin 'lavare' — to wash; used by Romans to scent bathwater.
Roman soldiers carried it for its wound-healing properties.

mint.habit: Vigorous, invasive herbaceous perennial spreading via underground runners.
mint.features: Square stems and serrated, highly aromatic bright green leaves.
mint.flowers: Spikes of tiny lilac flowers in late summer; loved by pollinators.
mint.conditions: Partial shade to full sun; prefers moist, fertile soil.
mint.care: Best grown in a pot to contain its spread. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage fresh leaves.
facts: In Greek myth, Minthe was a nymph turned into the plant by Persephone out of jealousy.
There are over 600 varieties of mint, including chocolate, pineapple, and ginger mint.

sage.habit: Evergreen sub-shrub with a bushy, spreading habit; 60cm x 60cm.
sage.features: Textured, pebbly, grey-green leaves; highly aromatic and soft to the touch.
sage.flowers: Spikes of bluish-purple flowers in early summer.
sage.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, even sandy soil; very drought tolerant once established.
sage.care: Prune lightly in spring. Do not prune in autumn as new growth may be damaged by frost.
facts: The name 'Salvia' comes from the Latin 'salvere', meaning 'to be saved' or 'to heal'.
Ancient Romans used it as a digestive aid and a memory enhancer.

rosemary.habit: Woody evergreen shrub; can be upright (to 1.5m) or prostrate/trailing.
rosemary.features: Needle-like aromatic leaves, dark green above and white-felted beneath.
rosemary.flowers: Small, two-lipped flowers in pale blue or white; often blooms in early spring and autumn.
rosemary.conditions: Full sun; sharply drained soil; sheltered from cold, drying winds.
rosemary.care: Prune after flowering to prevent legginess. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings in summer.
facts: Long associated with memory; students in ancient Greece wore rosemary garlands while taking exams.
In folklore, it is said that where rosemary flourishes, the mistress of the house is the master.

fennel.habit: Tall, herbaceous perennial with a feathery, airy habit; up to 2m.
fennel.features: Fine, needle-like bronze or green foliage; smells strongly of aniseed.
fennel.flowers: Large, flat umbels of tiny yellow flowers in mid-to-late summer.
fennel.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; very deep taproot makes it drought-resistant.
fennel.care: Cut back dead stems in late winter. If you don't want seedlings, deadhead before seeds drop.
facts: In the Middle Ages, fennel was hung over doors on Midsummer's Eve to ward off evil spirits.
The town of Marathon in Greece gets its name from 'marathos', the Greek word for fennel.

borage.habit: Hairy, sprawling annual that self-seeds readily; 60–90cm tall.
borage.features: Large, bristly grey-green leaves; the whole plant has a cucumber-like scent.
borage.flowers: Exquisite star-shaped, bright blue flowers with black centers; June–September.
borage.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; will grow in almost any well-drained soil.
borage.care: Sow in spring. Little care needed. Pull up plants once they become tatty; they will likely return from seed.
facts: The flowers are edible and a classic garnish for Pimm’s cocktails.
Known as 'bee bread' because it produces nectar so quickly that bees can visit the same flower multiple times a day.

rose.habit: Diverse; including climbers, ramblers, shrubs, and miniatures; deciduous woody stems.
rose.features: Pinnate leaves with stipules; stems often armed with prickles (thorns).
rose.flowers: Varying from single (5 petals) to fully double; highly fragrant; peaks June, often repeats until frost.
rose.conditions: Full sun; heavy, fertile, well-drained soil; benefits from mulching.
rose.care: Prune in late winter (February/March). Feed in spring and mid-summer. Deadhead regularly.
facts: Roses are one of the oldest species of plants, with fossils dating back 35 million years.
The rose hip (fruit) of some species contains more Vitamin C than any other fruit or vegetable.

elderflower.habit: Large deciduous shrub or small tree; upright and arching with corky bark.
elderflower.features: Large pinnate leaves; provides wildlife value through flowers and later, berries.
elderflower.flowers: Large, flat, creamy-white 'plates' of tiny scented flowers; May–June.
elderflower.conditions: Full sun to partial shade; tolerant of most soils, including wet or chalky ground.
elderflower.care: Prune hard in winter if you need to control size. Can be treated as a hedge or a specimen tree.
facts: Folklore warns that cutting down an elder tree without permission from the 'Elder Mother' brings bad luck.
Every part of the plant is used: flowers for cordial, berries for wine, and wood for whistles.

grape.habit: Vigorous deciduous woody climber; uses tendrils to scale supports up to 10m+.
grape.features: Large, lobed leaves with beautiful autumn tints of yellow or red.
grape.flowers: Inconspicuous green flowers in spring, followed by clusters of edible berries.
grape.conditions: Full sun; deep, well-drained soil; needs a warm, sheltered spot to ripen fruit.
grape.care: Prune in early winter (while dormant) to prevent 'bleeding'. Thin fruit bunches in summer for better quality.
facts: Vitis vinifera has been cultivated for over 8,000 years, beginning in the Caucasus region.
A single grapevine can produce enough grapes for 40 to 60 glasses of wine.

cherry.habit: Deciduous tree, varying from compact dwarfs to large canopy trees.
cherry.features: Glossy bark with horizontal lenticels; vibrant autumn leaf colors.
cherry.flowers: Masses of white or pink blossoms in spring (April), followed by fleshy drupes in summer.
cherry.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; protect blossom from late frosts.
cherry.care: Prune only in summer (never winter) to prevent Silver Leaf disease. Protect fruit from birds.
facts: The cherry blossom (Sakura) is a symbol of renewal and the fleeting nature of life in Japan.
The word 'cherry' comes from the town of Cerasus in Turkey.

raspberry.habit: Deciduous suckering shrub with upright, usually prickly stems (canes).
raspberry.features: Divided leaves, white beneath; fruit is an aggregate of drupelets.
raspberry.flowers: Small, white, drooping flowers in late spring/early summer.
raspberry.conditions: Full sun (but tolerates some shade); rich, slightly acidic, moist but well-drained soil.
raspberry.care: Summer-fruiting: prune flowered canes to ground in autumn. Autumn-fruiting: prune all canes to ground in February.
facts: Unlike many fruits, raspberries do not continue to ripen after they are picked.
The 'fruit' is actually a cluster of tiny individual fruits, each containing a seed.

strawberry.habit: Low-growing, herbaceous perennial spreading by runners (stolons).
strawberry.features: Trifoliate green leaves; white flowers with yellow centers.
strawberry.flowers: Peaking in May–June, followed by red fruit; some varieties (everbearing) fruit until autumn.
strawberry.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; benefits from a mulch of straw to keep fruit clean.
strawberry.care: Replace plants every 3 years. Remove runners to focus energy on fruit. Feed in spring.
facts: The strawberry is the only fruit that bears its seeds on the outside.
On average, there are about 200 seeds on a single strawberry.

fig.habit: Deciduous shrub or small tree; spreading habit with decorative silver-grey bark.
fig.features: Large, deeply lobed, architectural leaves; produces a milky sap when cut.
fig.flowers: Invisible (the 'fruit' is actually an inverted flower/syconium); fruits ripen in late summer.
fig.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil. Best with restricted roots (e.g., in a pot) to encourage fruiting.
fig.care: Prune in spring to remove crossing branches. Protect young fruits with fleece in severe winters.
facts: The fig tree is one of the first plants ever cultivated by humans.
In many cultures, the fig is a symbol of peace, fertility, and prosperity.

peach.habit: Small to medium deciduous tree; often fan-trained against walls in cooler climates.
peach.features: Long, slender leaves; beautiful pink blossom that appears very early in spring.
peach.flowers: Deep pink to pale rose flowers in March–April; fruit is fuzzy-skinned.
peach.conditions: Full sun; sheltered from frost; well-drained, fertile soil.
peach.care: Prune in summer. Thin fruit to ensure those remaining reach a good size. Watch for Peach Leaf Curl.
facts: Peaches originated in China, where they were considered the fruit of the gods.
A nectarine is technically just a fuzzless variety of peach.

apricot.habit: Small deciduous tree with a rounded crown.
apricot.features: Heart-shaped leaves; early blossom makes it vulnerable to frost damage.
apricot.flowers: White or pale pink blossoms in early spring; fruit is smooth or slightly velvety.
apricot.conditions: Full sun; very sheltered spot; well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil.
apricot.care: Prune after fruiting to avoid disease. Protect blossom with horticultural fleece on frosty nights.
facts: The apricot was once thought to have originated in Armenia (hence the latin name), but it likely came from China.
Dried apricots were a staple for travelers on the Silk Road due to their long shelf life.

lemon.habit: Small evergreen tree or spreading shrub; often grown in containers in temperate zones.
lemon.features: Glossy green leaves; fragrant white flowers; can have sharp thorns.
lemon.flowers: Small, waxy white flowers with a heavy citrus scent; can flower and fruit year-round.
lemon.conditions: Full sun; well-drained, slightly acidic soil; needs minimum 10°C in winter.
lemon.care: Move indoors or to a conservatory in winter. Feed with specialized citrus fertilizer. Avoid overwatering.
facts: A single lemon tree can produce up to 600 pounds of lemons in a year.
During the Renaissance, lemons were used as a cosmetic to redden lips and as a cleaning agent.

almond.habit: Medium-sized deciduous tree with a spreading habit.
almond.features: Serrated leaves; the first fruit tree to bloom in spring, often in February.
almond.flowers: Pale pink or white blossoms; fruit is a drupe with a leathery hull containing the nut.
almond.conditions: Full sun; well-drained soil; requires a long, hot summer to ripen nuts properly.
almond.care: Minimal pruning required; remove dead or diseased wood in summer. Water well during fruit swell.
facts: Botanically, almonds are not nuts, but 'drupes' (stone fruits) like peaches.
Almonds are entirely dependent on bees for pollination.

mulberry.habit: Slow-growing, long-lived deciduous tree; often develops a picturesque, gnarled shape.
mulberry.features: Heart-shaped, rough leaves; fruit looks like a large, elongated blackberry.
mulberry.flowers: Inconspicuous catkins in spring; fruit ripens in late summer (August).
mulberry.conditions: Full sun; fertile, well-drained soil; needs plenty of space as it spreads wide.
mulberry.care: Prune in winter only. Mulch in spring. Be careful where you plant, as falling fruit stains surfaces deeply.
facts: The Black Mulberry (M. nigra) was favored by King James I, who planted 10,000 of them in London.
Mulberry leaves are the sole food source for silkworms.

quince.habit: Small deciduous tree with a twisted, characterful trunk and branches.
quince.features: Large, pale pink blossoms; golden, highly fragrant, pear-shaped fruit in autumn.
quince.flowers: Attractive single pink/white flowers in May; fruit is covered in a fine grey fuzz when young.
quince.conditions: Full sun; moist but well-drained soil; prefers a spot near water but not waterlogged.
quince.care: Prune in winter to maintain an open center. Harvest fruit as late as possible before frost.
facts: Quinces are so aromatic they were used as room deodorizers in the Victorian era.
In ancient Greece, the quince was given at weddings as a symbol of fertility.

olive.habit: Evergreen tree or shrub with a slow-growing, architectural habit.
olive.features: Narrow, silvery-grey leaves; beautiful gnarled trunks on older specimens.
olive.flowers: Tiny creamy flowers in summer, followed by green olives that ripen to black.
olive.conditions: Full sun; very well-drained soil; very drought tolerant; hardy to approx -10°C.
olive.care: Prune in spring to thin out the center. Feed in spring. Can be kept in pots for many years.
facts: Olive trees are incredibly long-lived; some specimens in the Mediterranean are over 2,000 years old.
The olive branch has been a symbol of peace and victory since ancient times.
